items.q: Differentiate between `glOrtho()` and `gluPerspective()` functions in OpenGL.
items.answer:
| | **`glOrtho(l, r, b, t, n, f)`** | **`gluPerspective(fovy, aspect, near, far)`** |
|---|---|---|
| Projection type | **Parallel (orthographic)** | **Perspective** |
| View volume | A **rectangular box** | A **frustum** — truncated pyramid |
| Projectors | **Parallel** | **Converge** at the centre of projection |
| Depth effect | **None** — size independent of distance | **Distant objects appear smaller** |
| Dimensions | **Preserved and measurable** | **Distorted** by foreshortening |
| Arguments | Six clipping-plane distances | Field of view, aspect ratio, two clip planes |
| Typical use | CAD, technical drawing, **2D/UI overlays** | Realistic 3D, games, **VR** |

**Both** are set with `glMatrixMode(GL_PROJECTION)` followed by `glLoadIdentity()`.

> ⚠ **Never call both in sequence without `glLoadIdentity()` between them** — each multiplies into the *current* matrix, so the second compounds the first and the projection ends up neither cleanly orthographic nor cleanly perspective. This exact bug appears in the course's coloured-cube listing.

items.q: Construct a 2D octagon with the help of the `GL_TRIANGLES` primitive, ensuring the colours of the individual triangles are different. (The display callback alone is sufficient.)
Given the following 2D points, find the convex hull: a(3,5), b(5,4), c(−4,−6), d(−1,10), e(1,−5), f(6,−3), g(−2,−7), h(2,−9), i(3,2).
items.answer:
**Method — Graham's scan** (Unit 1).

**1. Anchor.** The lowermost point is **h(2, −9)**. It is guaranteed to be on the hull.

**2. Sort** the remaining points by polar angle about h.

**3. Scan**, keeping only left turns. Test each candidate with the cross product sign for consecutive points $A, B, C$:
$$(B_x-A_x)(C_y-B_y) - (B_y-A_y)(C_x-B_x)$$
positive ⇒ left turn (keep) · negative or zero ⇒ **pop**.

**Result — the hull, anticlockwise from h:**
$$\mathbf{h(2,-9) \to f(6,-3) \to b(5,4) \to a(3,5) \to d(-1,10) \to c(-4,-6) \to g(-2,-7) \to h}$$

**Interior points (discarded): e(1,−5) and i(3,2).**

- **i(3,2)** lies inside the quadrilateral a–b–f–d and is popped on the first right turn it causes.
- **e(1,−5)** lies inside the triangle c–g–h–f region and is likewise popped.

**Sanity checks:** every remaining vertex must be an *extreme* point in some direction — h is the lowest, d the highest, c the leftmost, f the rightmost. All four appear in the hull ✔ Traversing the hull, every turn is a left turn ✔

items.q: Simulate a camera with an adjustable focal length, which influences the field of view of the perspective projection.
Describe how OpenGL light interacts with material properties to determine the appearance of a 3D object.
items.answer:
The final colour at a point is the **sum of three contributions**, each formed by multiplying a **light** property with the corresponding **material** property:

$$\text{colour} = \underbrace{L_a M_a}_{\text{ambient}} \;+\; \underbrace{L_d M_d\,(\mathbf n\cdot\mathbf l)}_{\text{diffuse}} \;+\; \underbrace{L_s M_s\,(\mathbf r\cdot\mathbf v)^{\alpha}}_{\text{specular}} \;+\; M_e$$

| Term | Depends on | Behaviour |
|---|---|---|
| **Ambient** | Neither geometry nor view | A constant standing in for light bounced off everything else |
| **Diffuse** | $\mathbf n\cdot\mathbf l$ — the **surface's angle to the light** | **View-independent**; gives the matte appearance |
| **Specular** | $\mathbf r\cdot\mathbf v$ — the **reflection direction vs the viewer** | **View-dependent**; the highlight **moves as you move** |
| **Shininess $\alpha$** | Material only | Higher ⇒ tighter, sharper highlight |
| **Emissive** | Material only | Self-illumination; does not light other objects |

**Why the dot products.** $\mathbf n\cdot\mathbf l$ is Unit 1's dot product answering *'how aligned is this surface with the light?'* — maximal when facing it, zero when edge-on. $\mathbf r\cdot\mathbf v$ asks *'is the mirror pointing at me?'*

**In code:**
```c
glLightfv(GL_LIGHT0, GL_DIFFUSE,   lightDiffuse);
glLightfv(GL_LIGHT0, GL_SPECULAR,  lightSpecular);
glMaterialfv(GL_FRONT, GL_SPECULAR, matSpecular);
glMaterialf (GL_FRONT, GL_SHININESS, 50.0f);
glEnable(GL_LIGHTING); glEnable(GL_LIGHT0);
```

**Conclusion:** *neither the light nor the material alone determines appearance* — a strong specular light on a rough material produces no highlight, and a shiny material in purely ambient light looks flat. It is the **product** of the two that matters.

items.q: Explain callback functions in OpenGL. Give examples of how to register a callback function and how to use them within an OpenGL program.
Describe `glPushMatrix` and `glPopMatrix` in OpenGL, and state which sequence of transformation calls will first rotate an object and then move it to a new position.
Explain the `glLookAt` function in OpenGL with details and an example.
items.answer:
**Signature** (the GLU form actually used):

```c
gluLookAt(eyeX, eyeY, eyeZ,          /* where the camera IS       */
          centerX, centerY, centerZ,  /* what it is LOOKING AT     */
          upX, upY, upZ);             /* which way is UP           */
```

**The three vectors and why exactly three are needed:**

| Vector | Fixes |
|---|---|
| **Eye** | The camera's **position** (3 DOF) |
| **Centre** | The **direction** of view (2 DOF) |
| **Up** | The remaining **roll** about the view axis (1 DOF) |

That is **six degrees of freedom** — the same 6DOF that Unit 3's tracking systems must recover.

**Example** (from the coloured-cube listing):

```c
glMatrixMode(GL_MODELVIEW);
glLoadIdentity();
gluLookAt(0, 0, 10,    /* stand 10 units along +z */
          0, 0, 0,     /* look at the origin      */
          0, 1, 0);    /* +y is up                */
```

**What it actually computes.** `gluLookAt` **does not move a camera** — it builds the **view matrix** that transforms the world into the camera's frame, so the camera ends up at the origin looking down $-z$. Internally it forms an orthonormal basis:

$$\mathbf f = \frac{\text{centre}-\text{eye}}{\lVert\cdot\rVert}, \qquad \mathbf s = \mathbf f\times\hat{\mathbf{up}}, \qquad \mathbf u = \mathbf s\times\mathbf f$$

and assembles those as the rows of a rotation, composed with a translation by $-\text{eye}$ — Unit 1's change-of-basis, exactly.

> ⚠ **The up vector must not be parallel to $(\text{centre}-\text{eye})$.** If it is, $\mathbf f\times\hat{\mathbf{up}} = \mathbf 0$, the basis is degenerate and the view collapses. Looking straight down with `up = (0,1,0)` is the usual way to trigger it.

items.q: What is OpenGL's default coordinate system for objects if `gluPerspective(60, 1, 1, 100)` is used?
items.answer:
**The camera (eye) coordinate system**, with these conventions:

| Property | Value |
|---|---|
| Camera position | The **origin** $(0,0,0)$ |
| View direction | Down the **negative $z$-axis** |
| Up direction | **$+y$** |
| Right direction | **$+x$** |
| Handedness | **Right-handed** |

**What the four arguments define:**

- `fovy = 60°` — the **vertical** field of view.
- `aspect = 1` — a **square** viewport, so the horizontal field of view is also 60°.
- `near = 1`, `far = 100` — the clipping planes, at $z = -1$ and $z = -100$.

**Therefore only geometry between $z = -1$ and $z = -100$ is visible**, inside a frustum opening at 60°. An object placed at the origin sits **exactly at the camera** and will not be drawn — it is closer than the near plane. This is precisely the Three.js 'camera inside the object' black-screen problem, in its OpenGL form.

**The visible half-height at distance $d$ is:**
$$h = d\tan(30°) = 0.577\,d$$
so at $z = -10$ the frustum is about 11.5 units tall and, with aspect 1, equally wide.

> Note `near = 1` here is a **sensible** value. The course's cube listing uses `0.001`, which wastes depth-buffer precision and invites **z-fighting**.
